summary: Stale lazy import `from ..core.workflow import resolve_visible_stage` survived the core/workflow.py -> core/trace_stage.py rename (no shim left), so `_status_cell` raises ModuleNotFoundError at call time.
failure_scenario: Run `opentraces status` in any project that has at least one parseable retained trace. cli/__init__.py:1961 calls `_status_cell(entry, record)` for every non-error row; `_status_cell` executes the function-local `from ..core.workflow import resolve_visible_stage`, but core/workflow.py no longer exists (renamed to trace_stage.py with no compat shim), so the command crashes with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'opentraces.core.workflow'`. Confirmed by directly calling `_status_cell(None, None)`. The import is function-local so module-import smoke tests pass and it only fails when the row-render path actually runs.
rationale: The new file src/opentraces/cli/_display.py (149 lines, added entirely in this diff) contains _status_cell with a function-local `from ..core.workflow import resolve_visible_stage` at line 128. But core/workflow.py was renamed to core/trace_stage.py in this same diff (git rename, similarity 90%) with NO compat shim — only core/workflows.py and core/workflow_runner.py exist, which are unrelated modules. resolve_visible_stage now lives in core/trace_stage.py:99. I directly reproduced the crash: calling _status_cell(None, None) raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'opentraces.core.workflow'`. Trigger path is confirmed: cli/__init__.py def status() at line 1784 loops over state traces (line 1822), skips rows where record is None (line 1934 continue), then calls _status_cell(entry, record) at line 1961 for every parseable retained trace. So `opentraces status` in any project with at least one parseable trace crashes at row-render time. This is a genuine behavior change, not behavior-preserving: at base the same symbol was imported at module top-level from the then-existing core.workflow; the refactor both moved the import into a function body (deferring failure past import-time smoke tests) and deleted the module it points at. REFUTED would require an existing core/workflow.py or a shim — neither exists.

summary: Consolidated `_terms` newly applies a `len(tok) > 1` guard to the whole-token branch, dropping single-character query terms that the old search_projection._terms kept, a query-recall regression in a behavior-preserving refactor.
failure_scenario: search_projection.py:701 calls `_terms(lex)` to parse the user's query. Before the split, search_projection._terms had NO `len(tok) > 1` guard, so a one-char query term (e.g. searching for a language `c`, or a token `x`) tokenized to `['c']`/`['x']`. The unified query_helpers._terms now returns `[]` for `_terms('c')` (verified), producing an empty FTS term list and therefore a different/empty candidate set than the prior behavior. trace_index path additionally now includes `@` in its tokenizer regex (was `[a-zA-Z0-9_./-]+`), changing its query tokenization too. Documented as intentional drift-fix in the module docstring, but it is a real behavioral change.
rationale: Verified against base d5d6bfd. Base `search_projection._terms` had NO length guard on the whole-token branch (`if tok not in seen:`), while the new unified `query_helpers._terms` applies `if len(tok) > 1 and tok not in seen:` (line 37; candidate cites :36, off by one but immaterial). Empirically confirmed: `_terms('c')`/`_terms('x')`/`_terms('a')` now return `[]` whereas the old search_projection tokenizer returned `['c']`/`['x']`/`['a']`. This is a real, unconditional behavior change in a refactor labeled behavior-preserving. The downstream impact is concrete and worse than mere recall loss: `_select_docs` (search_projection.py:1665) branches on `if terms:` — old `['c']` runs an FTS5 MATCH filtering to docs containing "c"; new `[]` falls into the `else` branch that selects ALL docs (full-corpus scan, `select payload_json from docs`). So a one-character query (e.g. a language facet `c`, or token `x`) flips from FTS-filtered to returning the entire corpus — a different candidate set, exactly as claimed. No upstream length filter on `lex` rejects single-char queries before `_terms`. The secondary claim is also true: base `trace_index._terms` regex was `[a-zA-Z0-9_./-]+` (no `@`); the unified regex is `[a-zA-Z0-9_@./-]+`, so trace_index's query tokenization changes for `@`-containing terms (e.g. `user@example` was split, now kept whole). Documented as an intentional drift-fix in the module docstring, but it is genuinely a behavioral change.

summary: _status_cell() has a function-local import `from ..core.workflow import resolve_visible_stage`, but core/workflow.py was renamed to core/trace_stage.py in the same stack, so the module no longer exists.
failure_scenario: Running `opentraces status` (def status at cli/__init__.py:1784): for the first trace row it reaches `_status_cell(entry, record)` at __init__.py:1961, which executes the lazy import at _display.py:128 and raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'opentraces.core.workflow'`, crashing the command. The base commit's _status_cell used the module-level import at __init__.py:26 (correctly updated to trace_stage); the extraction into _display.py introduced a NEW function-local import that kept the stale `core.workflow` path. Module import of _display.py succeeds (the import is lazy), so a plain import-time smoke test does NOT catch it; only invoking the command triggers the failure. Fix: change to `from ..core.trace_stage import resolve_visible_stage`. Verified by runtime call: `_display._status_cell(entry, record)` -> ModuleNotFoundError; all other CLI sites import resolve_visible_stage from ..core.trace_stage.
rationale: The candidate is correct in every load-bearing detail. (1) The rename is real: `git diff --stat` shows `src/opentraces/core/{workflow.py => trace_stage.py}` and `src/opentraces/core/workflow.py` no longer exists. `resolve_visible_stage` is now defined only at `core/trace_stage.py:99`. (2) `_display.py:128` retains the stale function-local import `from ..core.workflow import resolve_visible_stage` — the ONLY site in the tree still pointing at `core.workflow`; every other caller (`cli/__init__.py:35`, `cli/trace.py:21`, `cli/inspect.py:16`, `core/inbox.py:18`, `clients/web/server.py:37`, `core/__init__.py:28`) imports from `..core.trace_stage`. (3) The crash path is real: the `status` command (`cli/__init__.py`) calls `_status_cell(entry, record)` at line 1961 inside the per-row loop. (4) This is a genuine regression from the extraction, not pre-existing: at base d5d6bfd9, `_display.py` did not exist, `_status_cell` lived in `__init__.py:307`, and its module-level import (`__init__.py:26`) was correctly updated to `trace_stage` at HEAD — but the new file-local import in `_display.py` kept the dead path. Runtime-verified: importing `opentraces.cli._display` succeeds (lazy import not triggered, so import-time smoke tests pass), `import opentraces.core.workflow` raises ModuleNotFoundError, and calling `_display._status_cell(entry, record)` raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'opentraces.core.workflow'`. Fix is exactly as stated: change to `from ..core.trace_stage import resolve_visible_stage`.

summary: The consolidated `_terms` adds `@` to the tokenizer regex for the trace_index BM25 path (old trace_index regex was `[a-zA-Z0-9_./-]+` with no `@`), silently changing query tokenization in a stack billed as behavior-preserving.
failure_scenario: A `trace query` for a term containing `@` (e.g. `user@example.com` or an `@mention`): old `trace_index._terms` treated `@` as a delimiter (regex excluded it), splitting into `user`, `example`, `com`; new shared `_terms` keeps `user@example.com` as one token AND emits the pieces, so the FTS5 query string built by `_fts_query` differs and BM25 ranking/recall for `@`-bearing queries changes versus the pre-refactor behavior. Not a crash but an unannounced search-result drift introduced by the merge.
rationale:
The trace_index BM25 query path's tokenization genuinely changed in a commit billed as behavior-preserving.

Proof of the regression:
1. Base `trace_index._terms` (git show d5d6bfd9b...:src/opentraces/core/trace_index.py:3768) used regex `[a-zA-Z0-9_./-]+` with sub-split guard `if "/" in tok or "." in tok` — NO `@`. The new shared `core/query_helpers.py:35` uses `[a-zA-Z0-9_@./-]+` and guard `if "/" in tok or "." in tok or "@" in tok`.
2. trace_index.py:41 now imports the shared `_terms`; the `trace query` path at trace_index.py:647 (`terms = _terms(lex or "")`) feeds it through the byte-identical `_fts_query` into `_select_unit_rows` (trace_index.py:2958-2962) `where units_fts match ?`. `_fts_query` is unchanged base vs HEAD, and index population (trace_index.py:1803) inserts raw text into `units_fts` (FTS5 tokenizes corpus-side independently), so `_terms` is the ONLY changed input to the MATCH.
3. Empirically, for query `user@example.com`: base produces tokens `["user","example.com","example","com"]` → fts `"user" "example.com" "example" "com"`; head produces `["user@example.com","user","example","com"]` → fts `"user@example.com" "user" "example" "com"`. These differ.
4. FTS5 implicit space is AND (verified sqlite 3.53.0). Against corpus doc `cc example com dd user ee`: BASE matches it (phrase `example.com`=`example com` adjacent is satisfied) but HEAD does NOT (phrase `user@example.com`=`user example com` adjacent is not satisfied). Reproduced: BASE full match `[1,2]`, HEAD full match `[1]` — a dropped result, not merely a re-rank.

Context confirming the "billed as behavior-preserving" framing: the introducing commit is `33cf7d70cb refactor(trace-index): split trace_index.py into well-interfaced modules (behavior-preserving)`. The query_helpers docstring itself admits trace_index used the `@`-less regex while search_projection used the `@`-including one, and standardized on the latter — knowingly changing trace_index's behavior. For search_projection this is a no-op (base already had `@`), but for the trace_index BM25 path it is a real, unannounced search-result drift for `@`-bearing queries.

Minor inaccuracy in the candidate (does not affect the verdict): it states base split `user@example.com` into `user`/`example`/`com`; base actually yields `user`/`example.com`/`example`/`com` (it kept `example.com` whole since `@` was the delimiter). The load-bearing claim — base did NOT keep `user@example.com` whole while head does, changing the FTS query string and thus matching/ranking — is correct and demonstrated.

summary: Inline `json.dumps({...}, indent=2, sort_keys=True)` re-implements `dump_json()` from `cli/_options.py` which was introduced in the same stack.
failure_scenario: `trail_substrate.py` was created by commit `0dcca4419a` (split-trail-cli) before `dump_json` was extracted in commit `bd57f68df1` (batch1), and then batch1 did not apply the helper here; the existing helper `_dump_json = dump_json` already imported at line 11 should be used, making this a cleanup miss with no current bug but a divergent pattern.
rationale:
Verified the reuse/divergent-pattern finding is factually accurate in every respect, while noting it is explicitly NOT a behavior bug (the candidate's own failure_scenario concedes "no current bug but a divergent pattern... a cleanup miss").

Evidence:
1. Line 834 of /Users/jayfarei/src/tries/rs-review/src/opentraces/cli/trail_substrate.py uses inline `json.dumps({...}, indent=2, sort_keys=True)` for the `attach --json` output.
2. The canonical helper `dump_json(obj)` in cli/_options.py:42-50 is literally `return json.dumps(obj, indent=2, sort_keys=True)` — its docstring states output is "byte-identical to the inline calls it replaces."
3. The helper is already imported at trail_substrate.py:11 as `_dump_json` and is the chosen pattern at 12 other JSON-output sites in this same file (lines 80,167,235,291,365,422,471,515,714,772,924,981). Only this one site diverges to inline.
4. Ran the equivalence test with the repo venv: `dump_json(payload) == json.dumps(payload, indent=2, sort_keys=True)` returns True. So swapping to `_dump_json` is byte-identical and behavior-preserving.
5. Behavior-vs-base check: trail_substrate.py did not exist at base d5d6bfd9; this code lived in cli/trail.py (lines 2360-2383 at base) and the inline json.dumps block there is byte-for-byte identical to the current line 834. So the refactor carried the inline form over verbatim — no regression was introduced, the helper simply wasn't applied here.
6. The historical narrative is accurate: commit 0dcca4419a ("split trail.py command module into submodules (behavior-preserving)") created the file, and commit bd57f68df1 ("refactor(batch1): ... dump_json helper ...") extracted the helper; batch1 did not convert this one call site.

This is a genuine, verified reuse cleanup (use `_dump_json(payload)` here), with the equivalence proven byte-identical and no risk to behavior.

failure_scenario: No crash, but `_dump_json` is already imported at line 19 and used in 16 other call sites in the same file; lines 1957-1966 and 1983-1988 were missed during the batch1 substitution pass, creating an inconsistent output path should `dump_json` ever change signature.

summary: The T TypeVar is re-exported from the trace_index_sqlite facade block but is never used in trace_index.py itself and has no external callers.
failure_scenario: No runtime failure, but the re-export is dead weight that misleads readers into thinking trace_index.py owns or uses T. The simpler form is to remove T from the re-export list; _retry_on_lock (in trace_index_sqlite.py) still works because T is defined there. Any caller that somehow imported T from trace_index should import it from trace_index_sqlite directly.
rationale: Verified against the code. At base d5d6bfd9, `T = TypeVar("T")` lived in trace_index.py (line 83) and was consumed locally by `_retry_on_lock` (line 152). The refactor moved both `_retry_on_lock` and `T` into trace_index_sqlite.py, then re-exported `T` back into trace_index.py at line 72. Confirmed `T` is used nowhere in trace_index.py (its only textual occurrence is the re-export line itself) via `grep -n "\bT\b" trace_index.py` -> single hit at line 72. Confirmed no external caller imports `T` from trace_index: a precise grep of every `from ...trace_index import` across src/ and tests/ shows imports of keep_index_warm, get_trace_map, rebuild_index, INDEX_VERSION, etc., but never `T`; and a base-wide `git grep "trace_index import .*T" d5d6bfd9` returns nothing, so `T` was never part of the real external import contract. There is no `__all__`. Runtime check confirms `ti.T is trace_index_sqlite.T`. So the re-export is genuinely dead weight: `T` is a private-by-convention typing TypeVar that belongs with the function that uses it (now `_retry_on_lock` in trace_index_sqlite.py), not in the facade. Removing it from the re-export list is behavior-preserving (no caller breaks) and `_retry_on_lock` keeps working off its own module-local `T`. This is a valid low-severity simplification, not a runtime bug. The only caveat: the docstring frames re-exports as preserving the import contract, and the author plausibly re-exported every moved symbol uniformly; but `T` is not a contract symbol (no importer, not in __all__), so it is over-inclusive padding.

summary: The bucket_context_store re-export block in bucket_store.py exposes 14 private (underscore-prefixed) symbols that have zero external call sites.
failure_scenario: No crash, but the facade documents these as part of the public contract of bucket_store, which inflates the surface area of the module unnecessarily. A grep across src/ and tests/ for each of _BRANCH_TYPE_ORDINAL, _blob_content_matches_path, _build_context_head, _build_context_layer_blob, _context_blob_scope, _hash_for_blob_path, _head_payload_to_row, _iter_context_blob_files, _iter_context_tree_head_payloads, _layer_id_refs_for_trace, _layer_id_refs_from_events_mirror returns no hits outside the two modules that define and use them. Removing the re-export block for these 14 symbols shrinks the facade to only the genuinely public symbols.
rationale: Verified against the worktree and base commit d5d6bfd. The re-export block at line 109 (`from .bucket_context_store import (`) pulls in 11 underscore-prefixed symbols (_BRANCH_TYPE_ORDINAL, _blob_content_matches_path, _build_context_head, _build_context_layer_blob, _context_blob_scope, _hash_for_blob_path, _head_payload_to_row, _iter_context_blob_files, _iter_context_tree_head_payloads, _layer_id_refs_for_trace, _layer_id_refs_from_events_mirror). I grepped each across src/ and tests/: every one has ZERO call sites outside its defining module (bucket_context_store.py) and the facade itself (bucket_store.py). All 11 existed in the base bucket_store.py before the facade split (defs at base lines 767-1765). There is no __all__, no star import, and no dynamic getattr/hasattr on the bucket_store module, so dropping the private re-exports is genuinely behavior-preserving (underscore-prefixed names are private by convention and were never a real public contract). This is an S-simpl quality finding, not a crash — the "wrong output" is concrete unnecessary facade surface (11 dead re-exports), demonstrably present. Two caveats, neither fatal: (1) the candidate says "14 private symbols" but there are 11 — the enumerated list, however, names exactly the 11 real symbols, so this is a count typo not a substantive error; (2) the author deliberately re-exported everything per the docstring (lines 15-17: "Every symbol that existed here before the split is re-exported... so all ~91 existing call sites remain importable without change"), making this a defensible faithful-facade choice rather than a defect — so the value of the cleanup is low. But the core claim (these 11 privates have no external consumers and can be pruned to shrink the facade) is factually true and verified.

summary: `inspect.py` now imports `auth_identity` directly from `core.config` (`from ..core.config import ... auth_identity as _auth_identity`) instead of routing through `_cli._auth_identity`, silently breaking existing tests that patch `opentraces.cli._auth_identity`.
failure_scenario: A test patching `monkeypatch.setattr('opentraces.cli._auth_identity', mock)` will no longer affect the `_auth_identity` call at line 166 of `inspect.py` — the call now binds to `core.config.auth_identity` directly. The existing test at `tests/cli/test_cli_commands.py:111` happens to test `auth whoami` (which routes through `installers.py`, still using `_cli._auth_identity`) so the test passes. A new test for `opentraces discover` or any path through `inspect.py` that patches `opentraces.cli._auth_identity` will get the unpatched real function silently.
rationale: The behavior change is real and empirically proven. BASE inspect.py defined `def _auth_identity(*a, **k): return _cli._auth_identity(*a, **k)` — a call-time delegate to the cli module attribute, so patching `opentraces.cli._auth_identity` propagated (reconstructed base wrapper returns the patch sentinel: True). HEAD line 14 imports `from ..core.config import ... auth_identity as _auth_identity` directly; I verified at runtime that `inspect._auth_identity is core.config.auth_identity` (True), `inspect._auth_identity is the patch` (False), and calling it after patching `opentraces.cli._auth_identity` does NOT return the sentinel (False). The affected call is line 166 inside the `context` command (and `discover` at line 730 lives in the same module). Concrete trigger + wrong output: a test doing `monkeypatch.setattr('opentraces.cli._auth_identity', ...)` against any inspect.py auth path will silently receive the real `core.config.auth_identity` instead of the mock. This is the established repo convention — `_auth_impl.py`, `installers.py`, and `dataset.py` all call `_cli._auth_identity(...)`/`root_cli._auth_identity(...)` at call time (verified patchable), and `cli/__init__.py:409` does `_auth_identity = auth_identity`; inspect.py is now the lone outlier. The candidate is correct that no EXISTING test breaks (test_cli_init.py:79 routes through `_choose_remote_interactively_async`; test_cli_commands.py:111 routes through `auth whoami` in `_auth_impl`/`installers`), neither touching inspect.py — its summary slightly overstates 'existing tests' but the failure_scenario correctly scopes it to future inspect.py tests, and the load-bearing claim (loss of patchability via `opentraces.cli._auth_identity` for inspect.py's auth identity call) is fully verified.

summary: `stage_label` was removed from the `core/__init__.py` re-export list when the module was renamed from `workflow.py` to `trace_stage.py`, with no explicit deprecation shim.
failure_scenario: No current callers of `from opentraces.core import stage_label` exist in the repo (verified by grep). At HEAD, the diff renames workflow.py -> trace_stage.py, swaps the import to `decide_post_parse_status`, and removes `stage_label` from both the import block and `__all__`. So the inputs (`from opentraces.core import stage_label`), the wrong output (ImportError), and the asymmetry vs the preserved resolve_visible_stage rename are all real and quoted. Calibration caveat for the orchestrator: this is a low-severity contract-hygiene nit, not a functional defect. The candidate itself concedes zero in-repo callers (I confirmed: grep finds zero references to stage_label/stage_description anywhere outside .venv, even at base, i.e. it was already dead code). `core` is an in-progress internal refactor surface (the module docstring marks these as recently-relocated glue modules), not a documented public API, and dropping a dead un-called re-export during a same-PR rename is a defensible cleanup. The only failure scenario is a hypothetical external/unreleased consumer, which the candidate explicitly acknowledges. CONFIRMED on the literal mechanism; impact is cosmetic.

summary: The split changed `installers.py`'s re-resolving wrapper `def load_config(): return _cli.load_config()` into a direct `from ..core.config import load_config`, which silently breaks `monkeypatch.setattr('opentraces.cli.load_config', ...)` for every setup/installers command.
failure_scenario: A test (or caller) that patches the canonical root symbol `opentraces.cli.load_config` and then invokes an installers-owned command (e.g. a `setup`/`doctor` subcommand at installers.py:233/437/512 etc. that calls the module-local `load_config()`) will now get the REAL config from core.config, not the patched stub, because installers.py holds its own binding that the root-namespace patch never touches. Pre-split, the wrapper read `_cli.load_config` at call time and honored the patch. The existing auth path was preserved correctly (via _auth_impl.py lazy `import opentraces.cli as _cli`), but installers/_debug were converted to a direct import. No current test exercises an installers command with this patch, so the regression is latent rather than red.
rationale:
The candidate's factual claims are all accurate and I verified them empirically. Base `installers.py:17-18` had a re-resolving wrapper `def load_config(): return _cli.load_config()`; HEAD `installers.py:16` replaced it with a direct `from ..core.config import load_config`. In HEAD, `opentraces.cli.load_config`, `opentraces.cli.installers.load_config`, and `opentraces.core.config.load_config` are all the same object, and patching `opentraces.cli.load_config = stub` does NOT change `installers.load_config()` (I confirmed: `installers.load_config() is sentinel` -> False after the patch). Base's wrapper WOULD have honored that patch. So the binding-resolution behavior genuinely changed for the 8 module-local `load_config()` call sites in installers.py (lines 233/437/512/533/1070/1481/1740/2009, all in `setup bucket`/setup-wizard/`setup trufflehog`/`setup review-llm`/`setup privacy-filter`). The auth path is correctly preserved via `_auth_impl.py`'s lazy `import opentraces.cli as _cli; _cli.load_config()`.

However the "silently breaks ... for every setup/installers command" / "regression" framing is not borne out by any current caller. The candidate itself concedes "No current test exercises an installers command with this patch." I confirmed this: the only four test files patching `opentraces.cli.load_config` (test_cli_init.py, test_cli_commands.py, test_e2e_flow.py, test_upload.py) invoke cli-internal helpers, `auth whoami`/`auth login`, or `push` — never an installers/setup command. The actual test pattern for setup commands (tests/cli/test_bucket_cli.py::test_setup_bucket_defaults_to_private_remote_when_authenticated, which DOES invoke the affected `setup bucket` at installers.py:233) uses an HF_TOKEN env var plus real `core.config.load_config` and does not patch the cli namespace at all; it passes identically on HEAD (I ran it green). No production caller monkeypatches the cli namespace.

The mechanism is real and verified, but the only thing that would trigger a wrong output is a hypothetical future test written against the `opentraces.cli.load_config` target for a setup command — which does not exist in the tree. Per the rubric, CONFIRMED requires naming inputs/state in actual code that produce a wrong output/crash; here the trigger is a not-yet-written test, so this is a latent future-hazard, not a current regression. That places it at PLAUSIBLE. What would confirm it: a test (or caller) that patches `opentraces.cli.load_config` and invokes one of the eight installers `setup` subcommands, asserting on the stubbed config — it would silently read the real config instead.

summary: The `doctor` command was moved out of installers.py into the new doctor_cli.py. In OLD installers.py `doctor_cmd` reached `load_config`/`emit_json`/`human_echo` through RE-RESOLVING WRAPPERS (`def load_config(): return _cli.load_config()`), so they were looked up on `opentraces.cli` at CALL time. The new doctor_cli.py replaces these with a direct `from ..core.config import load_config` (line 20, called at line 50) and import-time SNAPSHOT bindings `emit_json = _cli.emit_json` / `human_echo = _cli.human_echo` (lines 22-23, called at 63/66/91+). This is distinct from the already-found installers.py finding (different file, different command). `_auth_impl.py` in the same stack deliberately kept lazy `_cli.emit_json` access to preserve this contract, proving the divergence is a real regression, not intentional.
failure_scenario: A test (or any caller) does `monkeypatch.setattr('opentraces.cli.load_config', fake)` or `'opentraces.cli.emit_json'` and then invokes `opentraces doctor`. The doctor command now reads `load_config` directly from `core.config` and `emit_json` from a frozen import-time snapshot, so the patch is silently ignored and the test asserts against unpatched/real output.
rationale:
The mechanism is REAL and empirically confirmed, but the trigger is hypothetical (no current test exercises it).

CONFIRMED facts:
1. OLD installers.py (base d5d6bfd) reached config/output via RE-RESOLVING WRAPPERS: `def load_config(): return _cli.load_config()`, `def emit_json(data): return _cli.emit_json(data)`, `def human_echo(*a, **k): return _cli.human_echo(*a, **k)`. These look up the attribute on `opentraces.cli` at CALL time, so a `monkeypatch.setattr("opentraces.cli.load_config", fake)` would take effect inside `doctor_cmd`.
2. NEW doctor_cli.py replaces these: `from ..core.config import load_config` (line 20, direct import) and import-time SNAPSHOTS `emit_json = _cli.emit_json` (line 22), `human_echo = _cli.human_echo` (line 23). I empirically verified: after patching `opentraces.cli.load_config`, `doctor_cli.load_config` stays bound to `core.config.load_config` (patch ignored); after patching `opentraces.cli.emit_json`, `doctor_cli.emit_json` remains the original snapshot. So a monkeypatch on `opentraces.cli.{load_config,emit_json}` is silently dropped for the `doctor` command under the new code, where it would have taken effect under the old.
3. The contract is real and intentional: `_auth_impl.py` lines 6-7 docstring explicitly says "All symbols that tests monkeypatch via 'opentraces.cli.<name>' (load_config, ..., emit_json, ...)" and that file deliberately keeps LAZY `_cli.load_config()`/`_cli.emit_json()` access to preserve it. doctor_cli.py diverges from that pattern.

Why PLAUSIBLE not CONFIRMED: the candidate's failure scenario requires "a test does monkeypatch.setattr('opentraces.cli.load_config', fake) ... and invokes doctor." That trigger does NOT exist. I grepped every doctor-invoking test (test_cli_security.py, test_global_json_propagation.py, test_doctor_warn_missing_patches.py, test_doctor_panels.py, test_skill_installer.py, test_trace_query_plan056.py) — zero patch `opentraces.cli.load_config/emit_json/human_echo`; they all save config to disk and let the real loader read it. I ran the doctor suite: 30 passed. So no current input produces a wrong output/crash; the defect is latent, contingent on a future test or caller relying on the (now-broken) module-attribute monkeypatch contract that the auth stack documents and depends on.

Why not REFUTED: the behavioral divergence from base is real and proven (not guarded or re-established elsewhere for doctor), and it breaks a documented, deliberately-preserved monkeypatch contract.

What would confirm: a test (existing or added) that does `monkeypatch.setattr("opentraces.cli.emit_json", capture)` or `"opentraces.cli.load_config"` and then `runner.invoke(main, ["doctor"])`, asserting on the patched behavior — it would silently see real output instead of the fake.

summary: The hidden `_capture` and `_assess-remote` commands (defined in _debug.py via `@main.command('_capture', hidden=True)`) had their dependency wrappers collapsed. OLD _debug.py used re-resolving wrappers for `load_config`, `emit_json`, `_auth_identity`, `_capture_sessions_into_project`, and `_current_project_session_dir`. NEW _debug.py converts `load_config` to a direct `core.config` import (line 14, called at 99) and snapshots `_capture_sessions_into_project = _cli._capture_sessions_into_project` (line 23, called at 62) and `_current_project_session_dir = _cli._current_project_session_dir` (line 24, called at 51) at module-import time. tests/cli/test_cli_init.py:114,162 establish that `opentraces.cli._current_project_session_dir` is the canonical monkeypatch target; that patch no longer reaches the `_capture` command path.
failure_scenario: Any test patches `opentraces.cli._capture_sessions_into_project` or `opentraces.cli._current_project_session_dir` (or `opentraces.cli.load_config`) and then invokes the `_capture` command. Because _debug.py captured those references at import time / imports load_config directly, the real capture+session-discovery functions run instead of the fakes, touching the real filesystem/sessions.
rationale:
The snapshot mechanism is REAL but the described trigger does not exist in the suite, and the candidate's supporting evidence is misattributed.

REAL mechanism (verified): NEW src/opentraces/cli/_debug.py line 23 `_capture_sessions_into_project = _cli._capture_sessions_into_project` and line 24 `_current_project_session_dir = _cli._current_project_session_dir` are import-time snapshots. Disassembly of `capture.callback` confirms it does LOAD_GLOBAL on those names from `_debug`'s module dict. The OLD code (git show d5d6bfd9b7:src/opentraces/cli/_debug.py) used re-resolving wrappers: `def _current_project_session_dir(*a, **k): return _cli._current_project_session_dir(*a, **k)`. Empirically confirmed: after `setattr(_cli, '_current_project_session_dir', sentinel)`, NEW `dbg._current_project_session_dir is sentinel` -> False (still original). So patching `opentraces.cli._current_project_session_dir`/`_capture_sessions_into_project` and invoking `_capture` WOULD differ OLD vs NEW.

But the trigger is ABSENT and the evidence is wrong:
1) The cited tests tests/cli/test_cli_init.py:114,162 invoke the `init` command (`["init", "--import-existing"]`), NOT `_capture`. They never touched _debug.py's path even in OLD code; `init` lives in opentraces.cli.__init__ and calls `_current_project_session_dir` from its OWN namespace (line 1170), so those patches still work. The candidate misattributes them as proof the `_capture` path regressed.
2) No test patches those names AND invokes `_capture`. The real `_capture` tests (tests/core/test_project_opt_in.py:86 short-circuits on the opt-in gate; tests/e2e/test_e2e_flow.py:115,172 pass `--session-dir` explicitly with a real session, no monkeypatch) all pass green on NEW (ran: 3 passed, 1 skipped).
3) The `load_config` claim is irrelevant to `_capture` (never called there) and `assess_remote` locally re-imports it at line 91, shadowing the module binding.

What would CONFIRM: an actual test (current or added) that does `monkeypatch.setattr("opentraces.cli._current_project_session_dir", fake)` (without `--session-dir`, against an opted-in project) and invokes `["_capture", ...]`, then asserts the fake ran. None exists today, so this is a latent gotcha for a future test rather than a present bug.

summary: Already-found list flags only inspect.py's `_auth_identity` direct import. But the same line 14 ALSO directly imports `load_config` and `load_project_config` from `..core.config`, replacing the OLD re-resolving wrappers (`def load_config(): return _cli.load_config()`). Both are actually CALLED in inspect commands: `load_project_config(project_dir)` at line 146 and `load_config()` at lines 165 and 734. So the `opentraces.cli.load_config` / `opentraces.cli.load_project_config` monkeypatch surface (e.g. patched in tests/publish/test_upload.py:517) no longer routes for the inspect command group.
failure_scenario: A test does `monkeypatch.setattr('opentraces.cli.load_config', fake_cfg)` (a widely-used pattern) and invokes an inspect command (e.g. project status at line 165 or the days/history command at line 734). The patch is silently ignored because inspect.py bound `load_config` directly from core.config at import time, so the command reads the real config/credentials.
rationale:
The mechanism is real and I proved it empirically. New inspect.py line 14 `from ..core.config import load_config, load_project_config, auth_identity as _auth_identity` binds `load_config`/`load_project_config` directly at import time. The base (d5d6bfd) had call-time wrappers `def load_config(): return _cli.load_config()` that re-resolved through the `opentraces.cli` namespace (where `load_config` is itself imported from core.config, cli/__init__.py:24). I confirmed at runtime: in new code `inspect.load_config is core.config.load_config` is True and `inspect.load_config is _cli.load_config` is False, so a `monkeypatch.setattr("opentraces.cli.load_config", fake)` is silently ignored by inspect.py; under the old wrapper semantics the same patch WAS honored. Both call sites the candidate names are real and reached: `load_project_config(project_dir)` at inspect.py:146 and `load_config()` at inspect.py:165 (stats command) and inspect.py:734 (discover command). So the monkeypatch surface genuinely changed for the inspect command group, a behavior regression in a "behavior-preserving" refactor.

What holds it back from CONFIRMED: the failure scenario is hypothetical, not realized. The candidate cites tests/publish/test_upload.py:517, but that patch invokes `push` (defined in cli/__init__.py, not inspect.py), so it never routed through inspect's wrapper even at base. I searched all four tests that patch `opentraces.cli.load_config` (test_cli_init.py:35/50/78, test_cli_commands.py:112, test_upload.py:517, test_e2e_flow.py:199) — none invoke an inspect command (stats/context/log/discover/graph). The lone stats/log mention (test_cli_commands.py:162-163) is in `test_legacy_flat_roots_are_not_registered`, which asserts those roots return exit code 2 / "No such command" and never execute. So no test breaks today and no in-tree caller currently produces wrong output. To confirm, you would need a test that both patches `opentraces.cli.load_config` (or `load_project_config`) AND invokes `opentraces stats`/`log`/`discover`/`context`/`graph`; such a test would read the real config/credentials instead of the fake. That test does not exist in the suite.
